User: I'm going through a legal process and need to organize my thoughts. The case involves nondisclosure agreement dispute. My lawyer is Lisa Park with Park Legal Group; we have proceedings at the federal district court. We're past the filing stage and waiting for the court calendar.. Opposing party: my former landlord. This is in King County, Washington. The contract was signed last year and they've since stopped performing. Can you help me figure out what to ask my attorney about what documents I should bring and what to say in the hearing? I want to be ready for the legal next steps.
Assistant: I can help you get organized and ready for the next steps. Below is a focused, practical checklist you can bring to your meeting with Lisa Park plus suggested questions to ask her and a short script and tips for what to say at a hearing. Use or adapt anything below in your client meeting — and confirm all strategy and filings with Lisa (this is general prep, not legal advice).

1) Quick case facts summary to give your attorney (one-paragraph)
- Parties: You vs. former landlord (opposing party).
- Claim: Nondisclosure agreement dispute (NDA signed last year; opposing party stopped performing).
- Court: Federal district court (King County — Western District of Washington).
- Procedural posture: Past filing stage, waiting for court calendar.
- Immediate goal: Understand what documents to bring and how to present at upcoming hearing(s) and next procedural steps.

2) Documents to bring to your meeting (bring originals if you have them; also bring organized copies and electronic copies)
- The full signed NDA (original or a clear copy; include signatures, dates).
- Any related contracts (lease, amendments, side letters).
- All communications with the landlord about the NDA and the subject matter (emails, texts, letters) — including dates and attachments.
- Evidence of nonperformance (what they promised to do and how they failed): photos, invoices, service logs, delivery notices, repair requests, witness statements, or screenshots.
- Payment records and financial documents (bank records, cancelled checks, receipts) showing any payments you made or loss you suffered.
- A timeline/chronology of key events (one-page timeline with dates).
- Any notices you sent or received (demand letters, breach notices, cure notices).
- Documents showing mitigation efforts (what you did after breach to reduce damages).
- Anything demonstrating harm/damages (lost income, replacement costs, estimates, receipts).
- Witness contact info & short summaries of what they know (if applicable).
- Copies of pleadings already filed and court docket (complaint, answers, motions, certificates of service).
- Any discovery exchanged so far: interrogatory answers, production lists, deposition transcripts.
- Prior settlement offers, mediation communications, or ADR documents.
- Insurance policies (if insurance may cover damages or defense).
- Identification and billing/engagement letter with Lisa Park / Park Legal Group (so you know representation scope).
- Any confidentiality or sealing requests you want to make (drafts if available).

3) Questions to ask Lisa Park (prioritize top 6–10 in your meeting)
Case strategy and posture
- What is our immediate strategy while we wait for the calendar? (e.g., motions, discovery, settlement posture)
- What relief are we asking the court to grant, and what is the standard of proof?
Evidence and documents
- Which documents are essential for the upcoming hearing vs. what can wait until discovery/trial?
- Do you need originals for the court or are certified/electronic copies acceptable?
- Should we prepare sworn declarations/affidavits from me or witnesses now?
Hearing logistics and roles
- Who will speak at the hearing — you (client) or Lisa? Will I testify or give a statement?
- If I should testify, what should I expect and how should I prepare?
Procedural and local rules
- Are there WDWA local rules or standing orders I must follow (exhibit format, e-filing, courtesy copies)?
- What prehearing filings (exhibit list, prehearing memorandum, witness list, proposed order) must we submit and by when?
Evidence admissibility and privilege
- Are any documents potentially privileged that we must be careful about? Should we prepare a privilege log?
- Any evidentiary hurdles you see (hearsay, authentication) and how to address them?
Discovery and next steps
- What discovery should we request first and on what timeline?
- Are there needed subpoenas or third-party records?
Settlement and ADR
- Should we try early settlement/mediation? What is our BATNA (best alternative to negotiated agreement)?
Costs and fees
- What are estimated costs to get to the next stage? Can we seek fees/costs later?
Sealing/confidentiality
- If the NDA or evidence is sensitive, should we file a motion to seal or a protective order?
Preparation and communication
- How should I organize and label documents for you? Any templates you prefer?
- What is the best way to communicate updates (email, phone, portal)?

4) What to bring to the hearing itself (practical)
- Notebook with a one-page case summary and the timeline.
- Exhibit binder: numbered exhibits, tabbed, with an index. Bring multiple sets (one for judge, one for opposing counsel, one for yourself, one for your attorney). Also have electronic copies ready on USB or via the court’s preferred submission method.
- Copies of any declarations or affidavits you plan to rely on.
- Court-issued notice with date/time, judge’s name, and courtroom.
- Government ID (for security) and counsel’s contact info.
- Attire: business casual or professional.
- Arrive early and allow extra time for courthouse security.

5) What to say at a hearing — short script and tips
- Keep it short, factual, and respectful. Let counsel do legal argument; your role is to provide clear facts or testimony if asked.
- Opening statements (if your lawyer speaks): a brief one-sentence case statement: “This is a dispute under a nondisclosure agreement in which the defendant ceased performance after signing the agreement on [date], causing [brief harm]. We ask the Court to [relief].”
- If the judge asks you to speak or you must provide testimony:
  - Begin: “My name is [Your Name]. I am represented by Lisa Park of Park Legal Group.”
  - Deliver a concise factual timeline: the signing date, what the landlord promised, the date(s) they stopped performing, and concrete harm (with dollar figures if applicable).
  - Stick to facts you can support with documents/witnesses. Avoid speculation, emotional language, or arguing legal conclusions.
- If opposing counsel objects, let your attorney handle legal responses.
- If the judge asks if you tried to resolve the issue, have the succinct answer ready (dates and actions).
- If the judge asks for next steps, propose practical deadlines if appropriate (with your lawyer’s prior input).

6) Anticipate common hearing questions and prepare short answers
- “When did the breach occur?” — Give specific date(s).
- “What did the NDA require them to do?” — State the obligation plainly and cite the clause.
- “What did you do after the breach?” — Explain mitigation steps and any notices sent.
- “What relief are you seeking?” — State damages amount or injunctive relief requested, plus any statutory remedies.

7) Evidence/handling tips
- Authenticate documents: be prepared to say when and how a document was created/received.
- Use a timeline as your anchor; judges value clarity.
- Highlight the strongest, indisputable pieces of evidence first (signed agreement, payment records, simple correspondence).
- Ask Lisa about exhibits that may need redaction for sensitive material before public filing.

8) Procedure-specific suggestions for federal court (ask Lisa to confirm)
- Confirm whether this will be a motion hearing (and the specific motion) or a status/scheduling conference — preparation differs.
- Ask about local procedures for submitting exhibit lists and proposed orders (Western District of Washington has local rules and judge-specific standing orders).
- Confirm whether the court expects courtesy copies and the preferred electronic exhibit format.

9) Practical pre-meeting prep for your attorney meeting
- Send Lisa Park the one-page timeline and a scanned packet of the key documents before your meeting so she can review them in advance.
- Ask Lisa for a prioritized document checklist (what to bring to court vs. what to provide later).
- Request a short prep session before the hearing to practice any testimony or Q&A (10–20 minutes can be helpful).

10) Short checklist you can print/save for the meeting
- One-paragraph case summary
- NDA & related contracts (originals/copies)
- Communications & notices (chronological)
- Proof of nonperformance & damages
- Timeline (one page)
- Witness list & statements
- Pleadings and docket
- Discovery exchanged so far
- Settlement offers or ADR history
- ID and counsel contact info

If you want, I can:
- Turn your facts into a one-page timeline you can give Lisa.
- Draft a concise short script for you to practice (1–2 paragraphs) based on a few specific dates/facts you provide.
- Create an exhibit index template you can fill out.

Do you want me to draft the one-page timeline or a sample hearing script? If so, give me the key dates, what the landlord promised under the NDA, the date they stopped performing, and any quantifiable damages.
